Oṃ, homage to the Supreme Deity!

The Śrī-Śrī-Karpūrādi-Stotra: O Mother, O Consort of the Destroyer of Tripura, those who recite three times this seed-syllable (*bīja*)—which consists of the letter *ka*, devoid of the middle and final vowels, joined with the moon and the left eye—[attain liberation]. For them...
For those who have attained all perfections, words—both prose and verse—issue forth spontaneously from the cavity of their mouths, as radiant as a cloud of darkness. || 1 ||
Commentary:

Oṃ. Salutations to the one whose body is pure knowledge, who possesses the divine eye of the three Vedas, who is the cause for attaining the highest good, and who bears the crescent moon. Śrī-Śrīcaṇḍī.

I bow to the Great Goddess, the Fourth State, whose form is Brahman; by the mere remembrance of whom one is no longer bound by the path of worldly existence. (From the *Gandharva-tantra*: To Kālī, the goddess who destroys Time, whose form is the seed-syllable *Krīṃ*.
I worship Kālikā, who is Dakṣiṇā, who can assume any form at will, who transcends all parts, and who is Time itself.
The Heart of Kālī.
Regarding the word *karūram*: through these five verses beginning with *karpūram*, the twenty-two-syllable mantra of the Vidyārājñī, which constitutes the subtle form of the Mahādevī, is extracted;
likewise, her method of practice (*sādhana*) and her majesty (*māhātmya*) are set forth.

This has been stated in sequence. In the sixth verse, the extraction of her various mantras is also described. And it is said in the *Kālikā-śruti*: "Then he attains her, the auspicious one, who is of the nature of Brahman, in the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*)."
[One should meditate upon her] whose form is the unified totality of Kāma, Repha, and Indirā. First, these [three] are tripled;
then follow two *kūrca* syllables. That *kūrca* seed-syllable is of the nature of the union of the void (*vyoma*) with the sixth vowel and the nasal bindu.
Having uttered that very same [syllable] twice, one then follows it with two *bhuvana* syllables; for *bhuvana* is indeed...

Having uttered that very [seed-syllable] twice in the form of a union with the Sky (Vyoma), the Fire (Jvalana), the Moon (Indira), and the Void (Śūnya), one should then proceed facing toward "Kālike" on the right; thereafter, having uttered the seven seed-syllables,
one should recite [the mantra] for the daughter of the Great Sun (Vṛhadbhānujā).
This is the most supreme among all mantras. And so it is said in the *Niruttara-tantra*:
"Now, O Great Goddess, I shall declare the mantra of Dakṣiṇākālikā, by which..."
Through mere consciousness alone, one becomes liberated while living.
O Goddess, it consists of ten million Brahmā-fires, is endowed with Nāda and Bindu, joined with the left eye,
and is the supreme beyond the supreme, the very nature of consciousness.
The single-syllable perfected vidyā, the queen of mantras, O Mistress of the Kula; then follow the three qualities (guṇas), the pair of kūrcas, and thereafter the pair of lajjās.

One should join the seven seed-syllables as "dakṣiṇe kālike ca"; at the end, one should add the consort of fire (svāhā). This is proclaimed as the Queen of Vidyās, the Vidyā consisting of all mantras, which effects creation, maintenance, and dissolution.

Furthermore, in the first verse, the single-syllable queen of mantras of the illustrious Kālikā, the seed-syllable *krīṃ*, is extracted; in the second verse, the single-syllable mantra of the illustrious Tārā, the seed-syllable *hūṃ*, is extracted; and in the third verse...
The single-syllable mantra of the illustrious Tripurasundarī, the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*,
has been extracted; likewise, the section on the secret practice (*rahasyasādhanaprakaraṇa*) of Kālī, Tārā, and Sundarī has been described, as well as this hymn known as *Svarūpākhyastotra*.

The view of the Kramadīkṣita masters and the lords of practitioners is that the *kakāra-kūṭa-stotra* should be recited in relation to the Three Powers (*triśakti*). And it is said in the *Tārārahasya-tantra*:
"As is Kālī, so is Tārā, and so is Nīlasarasvatī."
Likewise, Tripurasundarī bestows all desired fruits.
Whosoever, relying upon the doctrine of non-duality, should practice [this], he shall be honored throughout the three worlds; indeed, he is like the son of Tārā herself.
If one performs the practice here by creating a division between the two mantras, there is no atonement for him, O Goddess; indeed, he is cooked in hell.

And it is said in the *Tārādhyāna* and the *Kavaca*: "May she who arises from the seed-syllable *Huṃ*, who is the single-syllabled form of the seed-mantra *Hūṃ*, always protect my throat. Likewise, in the *Stotra* of Śrī Sundarī:
O Mother Tripurā, dweller in the triangular abode, O three-eyed one, for those who chant your very name as the syllable *hrīṃ*, and for those who daily mutter "hrīṃ hrīṃ" while reciting your title,
what indeed is difficult to obtain here in this state known as Tripurā?

And so it is stated in the Mahākālasaṃhitā: "One should recite [the mantra] concerning Śrīvidyā, Kālikā, Tārā, and the Triśakti. In reality, however, just as a single type of creeper can never arise from seeds of different species, likewise [it is not possible with] the syllables *krīṃ* and *hūṃ*.

Since a single uniform form cannot arise from seed-mantras that are distinct from the syllable *hrīṃ* and others, it is indicated by the three previously mentioned seed-syllables that the Brahma-vidyā is indeed the illustrious Dakṣiṇakālī herself, who possesses all forms.

O Mother, O you who possess the luster of a mass of darkness, as the charming Navīnajaladhara (the New Cloud) possesses the beauty of a dark blue cloud, so may he, like the New Cloud, refresh the earth scorched by the heat of the sun with a rain of nectar-like water upon his mind-born son.

The sense is that she makes even that [world] cool by raining down the nectar of her compassion upon the body of the practitioner scorched by the three torments, thinking, "I grant immortality. O Consort of the Destroyer of Tripura,
together with the three cities situated in heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld...

O Maheshvari, the power that destroys the asura named Tripura! [The mantra is formed as follows: from the word *karpūra*, the middle letter (*p*) is joined with the letter *r*; the final letter (*ū*) is the nasal *anusvāra*; and the vowels are the letters *a*, *u*, and the *a* situated after the final *r*. Thus: *Klīṃ*. (Note: The text describes the construction of the *Tripurasundarī* seed-syllable *Klīṃ*.

"Middle" refers to the *p* of *karpūra*; "final" refers to the *ū*; "devoid of the middle and final vowel" implies the removal of the inherent *a* of *p* and the *ū*; "middle [letter] joined with *r*" yields *pr*; "final" refers to the *anusvāra* (ṃ); "vowels" refers to *a*, *u*, and the *a* following the *r* in *karpūra*).
Because it is devoid of all [vowels] in every respect, it remains as *kra*.

Being accompanied by the half-moon together with the dot (*bindu*) and the moon (*indu*), and likewise joined with the left eye, that is, with the letter *ī*, it becomes *krīṃ*. That is your seed-syllable (*bīja*).
The cause of the body consisting of mantra is that those people who, with their minds absorbed in the meaning of the mantra, recite it three times— that is, repeat it thrice— uttering it mentally;
[this pertains to] those who have attained all perfections, having reached the eight siddhis of Śiva, beginning with *aṇimā*.

From the mouth-cavity, that is, the opening of the mouth, of the practitioners, words consisting of prose and verse— sentences composed of both prose and poetry— shine forth and manifest spontaneously, meaning they emerge effortlessly and with ease. Furthermore, it is heard as follows:

This *krīṃ* seed-syllable of the illustrious Kālikā is recited as the mantra "Karīm" in the Arabic language by practitioners following the religion of Islam with the desire to attain liberation; likewise,
those following the religion of Christianity [recite it].
The practitioners as well, desiring liberation through the *krāiṣṭa* mantra, constantly recite it.
Now follows its explanation of the essential nature. || 1 ||
Having bowed with devotion to the venerable sandals of the yogi Rāmānanda,
this commentary on the *Svarūpa* has been composed, bestowing pure bliss.

O Mother (*mātaḥ*)—so called because you measure out and bestow (*māti parimitaṃ dadāti*) [the fruits of action]—you who grant both worldly enjoyment and liberation through the distinction between those with desires and those free from desire. O Radiant One, whose luster is like that of a dark rain-cloud; for Śiva and Śivā, whose nature is space, their bodies appear black. Yoga...

From the Vāsiṣṭha: One should meditate upon Śivā and Śiva—the two who are Śivas—as being directly present in liberation, free from all [worldly ties], resembling the clear northern sky, and accessible through devotion.
The *Tripurāsārasamuccaya*:
Because she consists of condensed light whose nature is the quality of pure *sattva*,
and because she is the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), she is to be meditated upon as blue-colored within the three cities (*tripura*) of the Consort of the Destroyer of Tripura.
That Jīva who sports, from him is born this entire manifold universe;
he is the support, the bliss, the indivisible expanse, and that into whom the two cities (the waking and dreaming states) enter as a city.

The Kaivalya Upaniṣad: The sense is that you alone are the bestower of disembodied liberation (*videhakaivalya*), for you are the very power of Tripurāntaka— the destroyer of the three cities— who, by taking away the gross, subtle, and causal bodies, grants liberation from the body (*videhamukti*).
p.

4) Devoid of the middle and final vowels [is the syllable *oṃ*]: the vowel *a* is known as *sāttvika*, the vowel *u* is declared to be *rājasa*, and the vowel *m* is said to be *tāmasa*; by these three, *prakṛti* is expressed.
The two [verses] on the synthesis of knowledge.
"One should unite with the *khara* (the hard consonants) and contemplate the supreme, soundless state. Thus ends the *Brahmabindūpaniṣad*.

[In this context, the *mūlaprakṛti*, which consists of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, has the middle syllable *u* as its nature, representing the *rajas* quality; and the final syllable *m* as its nature, representing the *tamas* quality.]

Devoid of those two, consisting of the quality of pure *sattva*, joined with the moon and the left eye (the letter *i*), it is the solitary digit of consciousness-knowledge (*jñāna-citkalā*) because its form is radiant with the letter *ka*.
Through union with the letter of fire (*ra*), it is auspicious and composed of all splendor; by means of the long vowel *ā*...

O Goddess of gods, she grants the desires of the practitioner; and because of the extraction of the *bindus*, she bestows the fruit of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*). [From] the *Tantrakalpadruma*. And in the *Toḍalatantra*:
"O Goddess, the letter *ka* and the letter *ī* are the givers of wealth."
The syllable *ra* grants desires, O beloved; the syllable *ma* bestows liberation.
By their recitation together, O Goddess, she becomes the giver of the liberation of *nirvāṇa*.
Thus, the Śakti is the bestower of the liberation of *nirvāṇa*, as well as the granter of the desired objects of the practitioner.

The power of Māyā, in which pure sattva predominates, is joined with those two (sattva and rajas). That which fashions the world-expansion—namely, camphor—is the Saguna Brahman; this is the meaning. That is your seed [which consists of identity with that, the consciousness-awareness known by the single name of the Supreme Brahman].
And through the conjunction with my own power, I have attained the state of being the seed-soul.

The body is indeed said to be the unmanifest cause, as was previously stated; for within it resides the seed-form of the universe, from which the manifestation of the subtle body (*liṅga*) arises. [From the Devīgītā:
Though you are devoid of qualities (*nirguṇā*), you are the cause of the world, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*).

The sense is this: being joined with Māyā, which is qualified by individual souls (jīva), karma, and time, you have attained the state of being the seed-nature for the creation of the universe when the occasion for each soul to experience the fruits of their respective karmas has arrived. This is what should be said regarding you.

Those practitioners who constantly recite that which consists of pure being, whose nature is existence-consciousness-bliss, which is threefold— distinguished as *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa*— and likewise threefold according to the distinctions of the gross,
subtle, and causal states, and which is the form of the triple power (*triśakti*).

One should meditate upon oneself as having the form of Kālī. [The Kālyupaniṣad: The sense is that those who contemplate [the Self] as non-different from their own self obtain the fourfold aims of life—dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—even if they do not desire them. And it is said in the Viśvasāra-tantra:
In the *Kramastotra* of Dakṣiṇakālikā:

"O Mother, the Siddhas indeed chant these three seed-syllables of yours for the sake of liberation; O Mother, those very [Siddhas] who have taken refuge at your lotus feet become perfected even within three days. (1)
O Great Goddess, if a person of dull intellect should ever recite even once at the end of a *chandas* another seed-syllable encircled by Īśāna and the left ear with the moon, having conquered—

He who deludes for a long time even the host of lotus-eyed women—the Lord of Speech and the Giver of Wealth—is now manifest in the Half-Moon Crested One, who bears the most terrible child as his ornament. || 2 ||
Commentary:
O Maheśī, O Śakti of Maheśa, the Lord even of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra;
O Candrārdhacūḍe, O you whose crest is marked by the crescent moon! O... [the rest of the verse follows].
In the ornament of the great and terrible child, with ear-ornaments made from a most fearsome corpse-child;

"a person of dull mind" means a person of deluded intellect; "those nine," surrounded by the left ear together with the moon, refers to that long vowel *ū* which is accompanied by the moon-drop (*candrabindu*).
It is joined. *Īśāna* is the letter *ha*. By this, the one-syllable seed-mantra *hūṃ* of your second form, Tārā, has been extracted.
Having formed this pair as a couple, if one recites it even once at any time, then...

Having for a long time, throughout his life, conquered and surpassed Bṛhaspati, the lord of speech, as well as Kubera, the giver of wealth, that practitioner becomes exceedingly capable of enchanting— that is, he possesses the power to bewitch— the multitude of lotus-eyed beauties.

The meaning is that one becomes learned, wealthy, and handsome. And so it is stated in the *Tārārahasya*: "Because she delivers (*tārayati*), she is eternally Tārā; she who is Kālī is certainly she herself."
And in the *Kramastotra*:
"By reciting your two *kūrca* mantras, one shall become worthy of worship even by gods and asuras;
everyone attains wealth and scholarship—what more need be said, O Goddess?"
In that which is called "the higher and the lower. || 2 ||
An explanation of the essential nature. || 2 ||

O Maheśī, you who possess the great sovereignty consisting of creation, preservation, and destruction; O you whose crest is adorned by the crescent moon— for the eternal Śivātmā, who is formless and whose nature is time,
the mark of the moon is established upon her forehead because of her immortality.

O you who bestow the liberation of great *nirvāṇa*! O you who are the crest-jewel of the most formidable child! Just as a child, having abandoned hunger and fatigue of the body, plays with an object, so too does the wise man, free from pride and ego, rejoice in happiness. *Vivekacūḍāmaṇi*. Likewise:

In the *Brahmopaniṣad*: "Just as a child, free from desire, attains bliss. [The name] is used in addressing her who possesses ear-ornaments exceedingly dear to both the desireless practitioner and the changeless child who resembles Maheśvara.

The meaning is that the practitioner (*sādhaka*), being changeless in essence like a child, is exceedingly dear to her whose form is Brahman. Accompanied by the left ear with the moon (the vowel *u*), the letter *Ū* is Bhairava; Sarasvatī is the long-nosed *Dīrghaghoṇā*; she is the playful one (*vilāsinī*), the creator of obstacles, and the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
[She who attracts form. The Moon is endowed with these qualities: immortality, the power of bestowing speech, and the power of attracting form.

"The Lord (Īśāna) is a person the size of a thumb, like a flame without smoke; he is the lord of what has been and what is to be. He alone is the first, he is the Sovereign (Īśvara). — Kaṭhopaniṣad. Thus, "the Sovereign" is another seed-syllable [formed by the two seed-syllables of sound].

The awakener of the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśiprabodhinī*). The *Yāmala*: "The King of Mantras is produced from the union of Śiva and Śakti, having the nature of the causal state consisting of the seed-syllable *hūṃ*.
From that Māyā arises she who is embodied as mantra, delighted by supreme bliss. The *Gandharvatantra*.

The essential nature consists of Śiva and Śakti. If one ever, even once, recites it through mental recitation (mānasajapa) or contemplates it, then that practitioner, having become possessed of knowledge, higher realization (vijñāna), and wealth, is able to enchant the entire world; such is the meaning.

Those who mutter the seed-syllable consisting of a couple— the Lord residing in Vaiśvānara, joined with the left eye shimmering like the moon, O Kālikā, whose hair is disheveled— they slay their enemies and bring even the three worlds under their control.
O you whose face bears two streams of blood from the pair of corners of the mouth; O you who are the three syllables of the word "Trā"! || 3 ||
Commentary:
O you whose hair is disheveled, O you with loose locks! O Kālikā, whose form is Brahman! O you whose face bears two streams of blood from the corners of both your lips!
O you whose face is beautified by streams of blood flowing from the two corners of your lips!
You who abide in the fire-syllable (Ra) joined with the letter Ra;
you who possess the shimmering moon-drops (bindu) of the moon; you who are joined with the left eye, that is, joined with the vowel I; O Lord (Īśa)!

The letter *ha*; the other is the seed-syllable of Tripurasundarī, *hrīṃ*. The pair refers to the aforementioned seed-syllables doubled. Likewise, those people who recite the mantra consisting of the syllables of the name "Dakṣiṇe" cause their hater [to perish].

They slay—that is, they destroy—the enemy; they bring even the three worlds, including those situated in heaven, earth, and the netherworld (pātāla), as well as gods, humans, nāgas, and so forth, into a state of subjugation, meaning they bring them under their control. || 3 ||
An explanation of the essential nature. || 3 ||

"Vigalitacikure" means free from the transformations of playful gestures such as the arrangement of hair; that is to say, it is devoid of emotional agitation (*nirvikāra*). Regarding "Kālike": Ka is Krodhīśa, Mahākālī; Kāma is Ādideva, the Illuminator; Sripura is Ramaṇa; Vaṅgakusumā is Paramātman.
Brahmā is *ā*; [Ākāra is Vijayānanta]. Ananta is *la*; [Lagnendra is Pūtanā;
Pṛthvī is Mādhava; Śakra is the designator. Viśvātmā is *ma*; Mandabala is Bheru;
Bhairika is the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). Viśvātmā is *i*; [Iḥ is Sūkṣmā; Śālmalī...]*
Vidyā, Candra, Pūṣā, and Suguhyaka—this is the designation of her body. Or, [she is] Sūkṣmā, Brahmā, Ā, and Ananta; thus Kālikā, by this, is the Great Goddess who is devoid of beginning and end.

The meanings of "endlessness," "subtlety," and "being the soul of the universe" are indicated by the phrase, "O You whose form is Brahman, which is without beginning or end. And this has been stated in the *Adhūtārāmāyaṇa*,
in the hymn to Asitā composed by Śrī Rāma:

I bow to Your very form designated as Puruṣa— devoid of beginning or end, the nature of the self of the world, existing as distinct [from the universe], beyond primordial matter (prakṛti), immutable, and possessing an unmanifest body.
With her face like the sky from the two streams of blood flowing from the corners of her mouth,
and her countenance radiant with the streams of saliva dripping from both corners— here, by means of the stream of blood,
the quality of *rajas* (passion) is indicated; therefore, the Great Goddess is free from *rajas* and consists of pure *sattva*.
"Stainless within the supreme golden casket is the stainless, partless Brahman;

that pure light of lights, those who know the Self know it. Thus it is described in the *Mastakopaniṣad*. In the context of Tripurasundarī, however, [it refers to] the Great Goddess through the quality of *rajas*.
The red-colored form is well-known. Residing in Vaiśvānara, consisting of light,
joined with the left eye and with the power that bestows nectar (amṛta) shining from the moon, he is the Lord (Īśa) joined with Māyā,
whose nature is the quality of pure sattva.

The state of being the subtle seed whose essence is the Lord (Īśvara) is another, distinct aspect of you. Regarding the couple (dvandva): the syllable *ha* is the gross body (*sthūladeha*), the syllable *ra* is the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*), and the syllable *ī* is that causal self (*kāraṇātman*); thus, the syllable *hrīṃ* is "I" (*aham*).

The Fourth [Chapter]. *Devīgītā*. [The seed-syllable] whose nature consists of Śiva and Śakti, who are denoted by the sky (the letter *kha*), is of the essence of the seed-syllable (*bīja*). Likewise, in the south—in the southern direction—the son of the Sun (Yama) stands stationed; he, joined with the element of earth, fled under the name Kālī.
Because she is all-pervading, that Dakṣiṇā Kālī is celebrated throughout the three worlds.

The Nirvāṇatantra. And likewise in the Kāmākhyātantra: "Just as at the conclusion of a ritual, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) bestows the attainment of the fruit, so too is this Goddess Liberation the bestower of the fruit for all. Therefore, she is called Dakṣiṇākālī.
O lady of excellent complexion, the Puruṣa is said to be the right-hand [principle], while Śakti is described as the left-hand [principle].

"Having conquered the right [side], she who is on the left is the bestower of great liberation; therefore, she is celebrated in the three worlds by the name 'Dakṣiṇā'. Thus, the three-syllable mantra, consisting of the names used for invocation, is what is expressed.
Those practitioners who chant and meditate upon the form of Existence-Consciousness-Bliss, which bestows liberation,
destroy— that is, annihilate— their hater, including desire, anger, and other factors that create obstacles to their practice;
they bring even the three worlds, the triple universe, into a state of subjugation.

[They] cause [one] to attain. In the context of Śrīsundarī, however, the meaning is: "O Kālikā," that is, O Raktakālikā, the third Mahāvidyā, O Tripurasundarī; and it is said in the *Vṛhannīlatantra*:
This Kālī is Nārāyaṇī; she is Tārā, the bearer of the Void; she is Sundarī, this Raktakālī, as well as Bhairavī and Nādinī.
And so it is said in another Tantra:
"Kālikā is declared to be of two kinds, distinguished by her black and red aspects;
the black one is called Dakṣiṇā, while the red one is considered to be Sundarī."
"In the south" means worshipped by Dakṣiṇāmūrti-Bhairava. "In the three syllables" means expressed by the mantra *aiṃ klīṃ hrīṃ*.
And so it is said in the *Kramastotra*:
"O Maheśānī, because of the concealment of Your two-fold modesty, the fourth siddhi shall arise."

By the grace of the boon-granting ocean of compassion, the lord of men attains sovereignty. [Visualizing her] with a sword in the upper left hand-palms and a severed head below it, and with the *abhaya* and *vara* mudrās in the right hands—O Kālikā, who removes the sins of the three worlds! O Mother, O Goddess with manifest teeth, for those who meditate upon this manifestation of yours, the eight siddhis of the Three-eyed Lord are as if held in their very hands.
Commentary:
O you who humble the three worlds, O destroyer of the sins of the people of the three worlds!
O you whose teeth are revealed [buck-toothed], the supreme eternal one whose body is adorned with red [gems].

The *Yoginītantra*. And likewise, in the *Tārākalpa*: [One should meditate on her] who is nine-fire-fold (forty-five) years of age, dark-complexioned, with prominent teeth that inspire awe, and full-breasted; she whose teeth are revealed. O Mother, O Source! To those practitioners who grant liberation in the South, [reveal] the power of your mantra.

The three previously mentioned *kāla*-seed syllables, the two *kūrca*s—[where *māyā* and *lajjā* are the *hrīṃ* syllable and *hūṃ* is called *kūrca*]—and the two *māyā*s on the right; thus, in the form of these three groups, there is the accomplishment of the ten-syllable mantra, namely: *tathā kālike*.

Having recited the three-syllable mantra consisting of the name, [one visualizes] in the left upper palm of the lotus-hand a sword (kṛpāṇa), and likewise below, in the lower [palm], a severed head (chinnamuṇḍa) with its top cut off;
and in the right upper palm of the lotus-hand, the gesture of fearlessness (abhī).

The *abhayamudrā* and the *varadamudrā* on the lower palm of the right hand; and in such a manner—with a sword in the upper left hand and so forth—they visualize and contemplate the form of Trayambaka, Śiva. These are the eight *siddhis*.

"Miniaturization (aṇimā), magnification (mahimā), levitation (laghimā), and extension (prāpti); irresistible will (prākāmya), sovereignty over others (vaśitva), mastery (īśitva), and likewise another, the power of determining the state of the unmanifest (aprākṛtāvaśāyitva)— having attained these eight divine qualities that indicate supreme nirvāṇa, O tiger among men, he reached the end of the gunas."
[Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: The eightfold supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇimā*, become as if held in the hands of those practitioners; that is to say, they are obtained without effort. || 4 ||
Explanation of the essential nature:
O destroyer of the sins of the three worlds, O remover of the threefold physical, verbal, and mental evils of the triple universe; O you who have manifested your radiant teeth!

O She who, with Her row of white teeth indicating the quality of *sattva*— which is self-luminous— devours the red-colored, flickering tongue indicating the quality of *rajas*, and thereby destroys both *rajas* and *tamas* through the power of *sattva*; [addressing] Her thus.
