9) O Mother! O Giver of Nirvāṇa on the right! Your manifestation through mantra (*manuvibhava*) is the form marked by the three of your own seed-syllables.
Likewise, the form consisting of the essence of *sattva* and composed of two *kūrca* seeds;
and the form consisting of the *sattva* predominant in *rajas* and composed of two *māyā* seeds;
and likewise the form of *saccidānanda*, devoid of beginning or end, which is designated by the name "Kālike Kālike."
Having recited [the mantra] and meditated, you, assuming a female form— [or, O beloved, one should remember the Goddess in female form,
or one should remember her in male form; or one should remember the partless Brahman,
whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss]— with your own left upper hand.
Therefore, having swiftly severed with the sword of knowledge— the lotus-bladed sword— the entire bond of karma created through desire or lack of desire, one remains pure within the self.

In the *Śivadharmottara*, and likewise in the *Yoginītantra*: "O Śāmbhavī, having slain the animal consisting of sin and merit with the sword of knowledge, [the teacher] severs the snare of delusion for the desireless practitioners; then, with his lower hand, he [bestows] that which is free from passion, the substratum of the knowledge of reality."

You bear [the gesture] upon your head with your upper right hand, and likewise, with your lower right hand, you grant fearlessness to those who seek the fulfillment of their desires, as well as the boon of their heart's desire. For those practitioners who meditate upon You in such a form, [of them...]

The meaning is that the eight siddhis, beginning with *aṇimā*, become attained without effort. O smiling-faced one, having joined the first letter of the [first] group situated in fire (ra), the very charming crescent moon (i), those three, the pair of *kūrcas* (huṃ), the pair of *lajjās* (hrīṃ), and below that, the pair of *ṭha*s (ṭha ṭha).

Those who chant the mantra of the Mother, the consort of the Destroyer of Smara (Śiva), while meditating upon her true form, become possessors of beautiful eyes like the petals of a lotus—the very stage for the dance of Lakṣmī—and they attain the power to assume any form at will. || 5 ||
Commentary:
O lady with a smiling face, O woman who captivates the Destroyer of Smara (Śiva), O Mother! Those people who [meditate on] that which resides within the fire... [ro]

Red, wrathful, and the letter *ra*; fire is considered to be of the nature of light (*taijasa*). [This is the title of the tantra. Situated above the letter *ra*. The Moon, the three forms of the Goddess, Mahāmāyā, and Rati; and Pauṇḍravardhana. [This is the title of the tantra. The graceful (*lalita*).

"Bidhu" is the crescent moon (the bindu), and "rati" is the long vowel *ī*; joined with these two is the first of the classes (*vargādya*), which is the letter *ka* belonging to the five classes (*pañcavarga*). Thus, the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is *krīṃ*. That triad—that group of three—follows immediately after that.

The pair of *kūrca*s is the two seed-syllables *hūṃ*; the pair of *lajjā*s is the two seed-syllables *hrīṃ* below that; then *tatapa*; then the pair of *ṭha*s [i.e., *dviṭhaḥ svāhā*, the beloved of fire]. This is the enumeration of the syllables: the word *dviṭhaṃ svāhā*.
"Having joined" means having conjoined. "Your form, beautiful as the splendor of a mass of dark clouds," and so forth, refers to the form composed of your twenty-two-syllable mantra.

Meditating while reciting *krīṃ* for the head, O Goddess, and *krīṃ* for the forehead— this should be seen in the ninth chapter of the *Śāktānandatarangiṇī*— they mutter the twenty-two-syllable mantra beginning with *krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ* and ending with *svāhā*.
Those practitioners repeatedly recite the Queen of Vidyās;
they possess eyes like the petals of the lotus upon which Lakṣmī performs her dance and play—
eyes that are like the leaf-petals of that very lotus.
"Of such a kind" means they possess forms as desirable as those of the gods of the desire realm; this is the explanation of their own nature. (5)

O you with the smiling face, O embodiment of eternal bliss! O Consort of Smarahara—Smarahara is the Destroyer of Desire (Kāma), that is Hara; his Consort is Śakti, who destroys the desire, anger, and other passions of her own practitioners—this is the sense. O Mother, those who... [text truncated]
This is the great, great Brahma-vidyā; this vidyā is considered to be Kālikā, having attained which even the lowest of men reaches the liberation of nirvāṇa.
And so it is stated in the *Kālīkulasarvasva*:
"Whether with faith or without faith, whatever man should remember [Her],
having conquered the fortress [of the body] and misfortune, he goes to the supreme goal."

Whosoever are practitioners—even if they be the lowest of men—if they [meditate upon] that triad of yours which resides within the fire, consisting of radiant energy; which is exceedingly charming, endowed with coolness and beauty; which is the first of the classes [of letters], the primordial source of creation, and whose nature is pure consciousness.

It has a threefold form through the differentiation of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Afterwards, there is likewise a pair of *kūrca* syllables (*huṃ*), which is the form of *Śabdabrahman*. Then there is the pair of *sajjā* (*svāhā*) and the form of *Māyā-śabalabrahman*.
Having joined two *ṭha* syllables below that, there is *svāhā*, the illuminating power (*prakāśa-śakti*) of Fire; by means of that—
Together with that, one should always contemplate one's own nature, which is self-luminous, as the Self in the form of Kālī. — *Kālikopaniṣad*
And so it is said in the *Sahasranāmastotra*:
"He who praises Śivā while meditating upon himself as the very essence of Kālikā, and having visualized his Guru as equal to Śiva— he indeed is the illustrious Sadāśiva."
And so it is stated in the Yoginītantra:
"To him who performs self-contemplation, thinking for even a moment, 'I am Brahman,' the Goddess shall grant the fruit; its end can never be calculated."

One should always contemplate one’s own body as having one’s desired form; likewise, one should contemplate the entire universe as having one’s desired form. Those who, contemplating the non-difference of their own form from the individual soul (jīvātman), recite [the mantra] and meditate upon it, [they...]
Practitioners of the *Lakṣmīlāsyalīlā*—[as stated in the *Nirvāṇatantra*: "By the mere grasping of this, a man becomes Nārāyaṇa";
and in the *Śyāmākavaca* spoken in the *Bhairavatantra*: "Even Nārāyaṇa, having heard which, [becomes so]... even a woman [attains the same].
Having become Maheśvara, he caused the Lord of Yoga (Viṣṇu) to experience agitation. And in the *Nirvāṇadyatantra*:

"Through meditation one obtains everything; through meditation one assumes the form of Viṣṇu. [The term] *lakṣmaṇāḥ* refers to the grace of Śrī; *lāsya* is dance; *līlā* is play; and *ramaṇam* is dalliance.
This is the meaning: the sense is that *lakṣmaṇā* refers to pastimes such as dancing.
11) He who is the support for that [pastime] is the lotus-eyed one, the lotus-eyed Viṣṇu.

They are similar to that. And it is said in the *Devīmāhātmya*: "Śrī has made her sole dwelling in the heart of the enemy of Kaiṭabha; those who can take on forms at will are capable of assuming bodies according to their own desire, just as Puṇḍarīkākṣa [did]."

The meaning is that just as Viṣṇu, by his own will, assumed ten kinds of forms such as the Fish, the Tortoise, and the Boar, as well as the Mohinī form, so too can the practitioners of Kālī assume various forms according to their own will.
And it is said in the *Kramastotra*:
"Therefore, O Mother, hear from me this fruit of your own name; the virtuous declare it to be the fourfold aim (*caturvarga*).
Furthermore, by worshipping the three seed-syllables (*bīja*), one attains sovereignty over the gods."
The Lord of Sages.
Furthermore, those who recite the pair of *kūrca* mantras in that manner become perfected ones (*siddha*) in the form of Narasiṃha [or Viṣṇu].
Moreover, by reciting the two *lajjā* mantras, those people attain perfection through the mind. At the end, having added the word *vibhā*, it belongs to Vibhāvasu (Fire).
They declare this to be the extraction of that mantra. || 5 ||

Whether individually, in pairs, or even all three together— the supreme seed-syllable, which is the ultimate secret— they always meditate upon it and recite it, having joined it with his name. For them, O Goddess,
Kamalā dwells within the lotus of their eyes, and Vāgdevī within the orb of the moon that is their face.
O you whose neck shines intensely with a garland of skulls, amidst the dance of full breasts!
Commentary:

O Goddess, you who are radiant by nature! O you whose neck shines exceedingly with a garland of severed heads, O wearer of the skull-rosary! O you who are enriched with full breasts, O you of swelling bosom! [This is] the ultimate secret.

It must be kept extremely secret from those other than the practitioner. For each [mantra], one should first recite either one or two [syllables] encased within the three seed-syllables, or the name [of the deity];
for it is stated in the *Kālikā-śruti* that "one attains success through this. Or else, [one may recite] the previously mentioned [mantras].
For each of the seed-syllables— whether they be two, or two syllables, or three,

or even three syllables— one should join them with their name ending in the vocative case, namely the name "Dakṣiṇakālikā," and thus enclose the one-syllable, two-syllable, or three-syllable [mantra] within it.

Or, one may meditate upon the entire Vidyārājñī consisting of twenty-two syllables. As stated in the *Bhūtaśuddhi-tantra*: "Whatever deity is prescribed for whichever mantra, having mentally visualized that form, one should perform the recitation (*japa*)."

Those who meditate upon your form— described in the *Adhyā* [chapter] as being expressed by that very mantra, dark blue like a fresh cloud, naked, possessing full breasts, wearing a garland of severed heads, and with disheveled hair—
and recite even a single mantra from among the previously mentioned mantras, for them...
In the lotus-eye—the lotus of the eye—of practitioners, Kamalā, that is Lakṣmī, always sports; she ever abides there. (p.

Likewise, upon the orb of the moon-like faces of those [who worship], which is bright with the rays [emanating] from their mouths, the Goddess of Speech, Sarasvatī, sports—that is, she dwells there. The sense is that they become possessed of wealth and possessed of knowledge. In the *Śrīsundarī* tradition, however: "O Goddess Tripurasundarī!"

Those practitioners who, having joined the three-syllable seed-mantra *sakalam* with your name *hrīṃ*, [recite] either the mantra known as the Śakti-kūṭa as *sakalahrīṃ* alone for each, or together with the Kāmarāja-kūṭa—

Meditating upon you—the King of Mantras consisting of fifteen syllables, which comprises either two *kūṭas* or the three *kūṭas* known as Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, and Śakti—they perform recitation (*japa*). For them, "the eyes, the arrows, the Vedas," and so forth, is all as before. 6.
Explanation of the essential nature. || 6 ||

O Goddess, whose nature is self-luminous! O You whose neck shines exceedingly with a garland of severed heads! O You who consist of the fifty phonemes! [The *Niruttaratantra* says: "Residing upon my neck is a garland of fifty severed heads, smeared with dripping blood."
The seed-syllable consists of the fifty letters; it is the *Kāmadhenu-tantra*. And likewise, in the *Viśvamāra-tantra*:
"Brahman, consisting of supreme bliss, adorned with the Brahman of Sound, [resides] within the body of the self."
O Dear One, it is the essence of all mantras.

And in the Rādhātantra: "The fifty letters of the Mātṛkā, beginning with 'A' and ending with 'Kṣa', are imperishable, unlimited, and situated within the throat of Tripurā; they possess a white luster and a red hue."

[She who has a yellow luster and a black form. O you whose form is the Śabdabrahman! O you, O Goddess endowed with full breasts, who protect the three worlds by providing nourishment in the form of breast milk and other sustenance, and likewise grant liberation to practitioners by bestowing the nectar of your milk! O Mother, yours—

Each one, or the pair, or even all three together— O Lord, your seed-syllable (bīja) is the most supreme secret, comprising everything with its qualities; it is the individual form known as Prājña, Taijasa, and Viśva,
as well as the collective forms known as Īśa, Sūtra, and Virāṭ.
The wise one is the causal self (kāraṇātmā), while the subtle-bodied is the taijasa;
the gross-bodied is known as the viśva—thus it is proclaimed to be threefold.

Thus the Lord is also described by the words "Lord" (*īśa*), "Sūtra," and "Virāṭ. The first is of the nature of the individual (*vyaṣṭi*), while the other is remembered as the universal self (*samaṣṭy-ātman*). [Devīgītā:
Contemplating [the truth], they chant [it] and constantly reflect through hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*).

In the lotus-eyes of those practitioners of the yoga of knowledge, the Goddess Kamalā sports; in their mouths, which are the abode of the goddess of speech, she dwells as if having taken up residence with firm stability, having drunk the very essence of the end of existence. — *Bhairavatantra*.

The sense is that by their compassionate glance, they bestow wealth and sovereignty even upon others; what need is there to mention themselves? Furthermore, the sense is that the Goddess of Speech sports within the orb of their moon-like faces, and thus their speech becomes composed of prose-lotuses. Or else:

O Mother, those practitioners who, contemplating your entire qualified form consisting of the Śabdabrahman as non-different from their own self, recite these mantras— for them, [the results manifest] in the lotus of their eyes, and so forth. || 9 ||
(13) [I bow to her] whose hips shine with a girdle formed by the multitude of arms of the lifeless, who is clothed in the directions,
the creator of the three worlds, the three-eyed one, resting upon a funeral pyre in the cremation ground on the heart of a corpse.

O Mother, even one of dull intellect becomes a poet and a commentator by meditating upon you as you are engaged in amorous play with Mahākāla. O Mother, creator of the three worlds! [This refers to] those whose life-breath has departed—the dead.
Her hips resplendent with girdles fashioned in many ways, her buttocks beautified by waist-ornaments formed by a multitude of hands; clad in the directions as her garment,
the naked one, the creator of the three worlds and of the triple universe.

She who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; she who has three eyes; because Kālikā perceives the entire universe through the three—namely the moon, the sun, and fire—therefore the three eyes are conceived. [From the *Mahānirvāṇatantra*: She whose eyes are the moon, the sun, and fire.
Upon a couch situated in a cremation ground— the heart of a corpse,
which serves as the bed for Sadāśiva in the form of a corpse lying in the cemetery—
she is engaged in the great rite of love with Mahākāla, through amorous sports together with Paramaśiva.
Meditating upon you—that is, reflecting on you—a person, even if dull-witted and of slow intellect, becomes a poet, skilled in the composition of poetry. || 7 ||
An explanation of the essential nature. || 7 ||

O Mother, creator of all things moving and unmoving! Your hips are radiant with a girdle fashioned from the multitude of arms of those whose life-breath has departed. "By action alone is a being born;
by action alone one dissolves. When the body is destroyed, that very action is obtained again in another body."

Great Nirvāṇa. And in the Śrī-Śrī-Bevī-Gītā: "In that [state], the actions, the individual souls, and time of living beings move about; they become merged without distinction, like the state of deep sleep during worldly activity."

"Having created the entire world, may I not enter into its midst, accompanied by Māyā, Karma, and the rest, O Mountain, with Pāṇapurī at my head. At the end of the Kalpa, all living beings, having abandoned their gross bodies along with their respective karmas, [enter the subtle state].

Having resorted to the *liṅgadeha*, they remain within the portion consisting of ignorance (*avidyā*) of the causal body (*kāraṇadeha*), which is of the nature of the qualified Brahman (*saguṇabrahma*), until the beginning of a new kalpa or until liberation;
for this very reason, here [are mentioned] the deceased living beings.

The sense is that a girdle is fashioned upon the upper region of the hips of the Great Goddess Virāṭrūpā, who possesses a sunken belly suitable for conceiving a fetus and a corresponding womb, by means of the multitude of rays serving as the primary instruments of action. She is clothed in the directions (Digvastrā).
"Vastra" means the veil of illusion (māyāvaraṇa); by that [veil], she is empty, meaning she transcends illusion.

Furthermore, she is the sustainer of the three worlds, [providing] for living beings at the beginning of a kalpa their rebirths and enjoyments according to the karma accumulated under her own control.

The creator of the ritual ordinance; the three-eyed one; the knower of the three times; [even the great beings dwelling in the cremation ground, when the dissolution has arrived, lie down as if they were corpses, and thus it becomes a cremation ground]; in the great dissolution, all beings.
That place in which those in the form of corpses sleep and dissolve is the Great Space (mahākāśa).
Upon that bed, which is the heart of a corpse— in this context, the syllable *śava* denotes Brahman according to the *Pretanirṇaya*.
The Gāyatrī Tantra and the Gandharva Tantra state:
"O Supreme Goddess, that which is Śambhu is indeed Śrī Sadāśiva; above him, O Maheśānī, is the subtle Tripurasundarī. Here, "Śava" refers to the Nirguṇa Brahman as the bed or support.

The meaning is: while she remains established in her own station, which is the substratum of the form of the attributeless Brahman (nirguṇabrahma) and is itself the form of the attributeless Brahman; [she remains] with Paramaśiva at the end of the kalpa, engaged in union with Mahākāla, because of the absence of activities such as creation and because of being devoid of action.
Experiencing indivisible, unfragmented bliss; meditating thus upon You,
whose nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss (Saccidānanda), and making You manifest through contemplation—
even a person of dull intellect, whose mind is seized by passion for sense objects— becomes a poet, a possessor of great wisdom.
It exists; thus it is called "being" (bhāva). || 7 ||

Somewhere, they always meditate upon you— the youthful consort of Śiva— who, having entered a funeral pyre made manifest, intensely crowded with auspicious yet terrible throngs of corpses and heaps of skulls and bones, remains ever satisfied by the divine sexual union above.
And there is no contempt for them. || 8 ||
Commentary:
By "ghorābhiḥ" is meant by the terrifying; by "śivābhiḥ" is meant by jackals;
and by "śavanivahamuṇḍāsthinikaraiḥ" is meant by the heaps of skulls from the multitudes of corpses.
And with skeletons; "supremely" means exceedingly; "in the crowded" means in the packed;
"entered into the manifest funeral pyre" means having made her enter, that is, standing in the midst of the cremation fire; [and] satisfied by sexual union on top.

Together with Mahākāla, she rejoices in a state of inverted conduct; though exceedingly youthful, she remains eternally fresh for all the worlds, as if still in her youth, despite having transcended both childhood and old age.
[From the *Śāradātilaka*:

"Those who constantly meditate upon you— the consort of Śiva, the deluder of Time— without ceasing, for those practitioners of yours, there shall be no contempt or disregard anywhere here, whether in this world or in the scriptures."]
The meaning is that it would not exist.
An explanation of the essential nature. || 8 ||
With terrible, fearsome, and exceedingly invincible jackals— meaning those of an auspicious nature (*śiva-prakṛti*) composed of the unquintuplicated great elements (*apañcīkṛta-mahābhūta*)—
and with heaps of corpses and collections of skulls and bones; here, [the reference is] to skeletons of bones.

By its white color, the quality of *sattva* is indicated; therefore, [it is joined] with the collection of qualities such as *sattva* belonging to the souls of those who have died during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*),
in that which is supremely mixed and utterly crowded.
In the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), which is self-luminous by nature and which, in the form of consciousness, stands pervading this entire manifest world—[namely, Śrī Śrī Caṇḍī].
Having entered and being empowered, she is satisfied by the supreme sexual union. "She who, having conquered the right [side], bestows great liberation" (*Nirvāṇatantra*).
Likewise, in the *Gandharvatantro*:
Having placed the Puruṣa below her, she whose nature is the half-syllable *ha* sports in the reverse manner, she who is the embodiment of fire, the moon,
and the sun.
And in the Niruttara Tantra:
"Kālī, who is the delight in the reverse order, is without qualities when she possesses qualities."
And in the Vāsiṣṭha Rāmāyaṇa: "Creation is the state of having a nature other than one's own; Śiva is the state of being of one essence with his own nature.
[Thus,] having transcended Paramaśiva, by his own will, he engages in the activities of creation, maintenance, dissolution, and so forth.

[She is] sporting; [she is] exceedingly youthful; [she is] always possessed of a single nature, meaning she is immutable. She is the consort of Hara—Hara being so called because he removes (*harati*) the three-fold suffering of living beings by bestowing the knowledge of reality—and she is his Śakti (power); [she is] that [Śakti] of living beings...

The meaning is "the bestower of liberation. Those practitioners who always meditate upon You—who are thus constituted of consciousness and bliss—with a steady mind day after day, and thereby perceive You directly; for them, in any birth whatsoever, there is no humiliation.
Such a birth does not lead to rebirth; they attain nirvāṇa and liberation—this is the meaning. || 8 ||

O Mother, what shall we say to you? We are indeed of dull intellect; neither the Creator, nor the Lord, nor even Hari knows your supreme nature. Nevertheless, devotion to you makes us speak incessantly;
therefore, this must be forgiven, for surely the anger of a cowherd’s daughter is not intended for those who look upon her as a beast.
Commentary:
O Immeasurable One! [The word *amā* may mean "without qualities" (*nirguṇa*); that too is the unceasing Sarasvatī.]
The Unsurpassed Tantra.
In the Mahākālasaṃhitā:
"She whose essential nature is inconceivable, immeasurable, and manifold power; she who, as the singular embodiment of existence, presides over every individual being."
You alone are established as the Supreme Brahman, accessible solely through non-dual realization that transcends all qualities (*guṇātīta-nirdvandva-bodha*).

O Mother, O progenitress of the three worlds, even the Creator Brahmā does not know— does not perceive— your supreme, ultimate reality (*parama-yathārtha-tattva*), which is devoid of all limitation (*iyattā-rahita*).

Even Īśa Rudra does not know [this], nor does Hari Viṣṇu understand it; we, who are exceedingly dull-witted and of slow intellect, what can we say or speak regarding Your nature? Nevertheless, despite our ignorance, there is devotion to You.
An activity directed toward praise; it makes us talkative, impelling us toward words of eulogy. For that reason, this act of ours is unworthy of you.
It must be forgiven—that is, endured—certainly. [This applies to] the anger of one who looks upon others with compassion, regarding their ignorance.
Anger is neither appropriate nor fitting. || 9 ||
(16) Explanation of the Essential Nature || 9 ||
O Immeasurable One, devoid of the limitation of qualities— that is, O Attributeless One— O Mother,
You who are both one and many, subtle and formless, give birth to millions upon millions of cosmic eggs;
who am I, what is Viṣṇu, or what is the other known as Śiva, and what are the other gods?
You are capable of praising Bhava and Īśāna. Thus it is said in the Devīsūkta:
"The assumption of bodies by Viṣṇu and also by me, Īśāna, was caused by you. And likewise in the Devīmāhātmya:
"Viṣṇoḥ śarīragrahaṇamahamīśāna eva ca | kāritāste..."
Therefore, who would be capable of praising you?
And in the Viṣṇuyāmala:
"O Mother, no one knows Your supreme form;
the gods worship that form which resides in places such as Kālī."
Furthermore, in the Mahākālī-stotra:
"When there was neither Dhātṛ, nor Viṣṇu, nor Rudra, nor Kālī, nor even the five elements,
then you alone were the single form consisting of the causal Sattva."

[Established as the form of the Supreme Brahman. O Creator of us and of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and others! Therefore, even Brahmā—the ordainer of birth and so forth for living beings according to their karma—does not know Your supreme, ultimate reality (*paramatattva*). He does not know it.

He knows. Even Īśa—Rudra, endowed with the power of sovereignty (aiśī-śakti)—does not know; nor does Hari—Viṣṇu, the remover of the three-fold afflictions of living beings—know. Since you are the mother even of them, therefore, [only you possess] the knowledge of the true nature of your own essence as the Mother of the World (Jaganmātṛ).
How could there be knowledge of the birth, deeds, and so forth of one's own mother among these?
The meaning is that such a thing is utterly impossible for [ordinary] continuums. We are of dull intellect;
what can we say, since even the lords of gods, beginning with Brahmā, do not know Your true nature?
The sense is: "We, possessing only worldly knowledge, know but a little; how then can we be capable of describing Your true nature?
Nevertheless, devotion to You makes me garrulous in the narration of Your qualities, even though I am unfit for such a task. Even so, [I shall speak] of You.
Devotion directed toward the object inspires us slightly to speak of its qualities;
therefore, this [criticism] of ours must be forgiven, for resentment toward one’s own herd is neither fitting nor appropriate.
If a young woman, whose breasts and hips are plump on all sides, being attached to pleasure, should at night recite your hymn with devotion while naked, meditating upon you with her hair disheveled,
then all the hosts of *siddhas* on earth will come under her control; such a poet lives for a very long time.
Commentary:
O Mother, the devotee who has received consecration, being a mantra-practitioner, should perform the family worship (kulapūjā).

O Goddess, without the conduct of one’s family (kulācāra), the mantra of Kālī is not accomplished. [This is the unsurpassed teaching. Your practitioner, devoted to the conduct of heroes (vīrācāra), if at night [during the evening] he lies down naked, well-established in sexual union, or with his hair disheveled—of him...
The accomplishment of all aims. Phetkāriṇī.
And in the Kālīkrama:

"One devoted to one's own conduct should always recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times by day as a *paśu*; or else, whether a *divya* or a *vīra*, one should perform the recitation of one hundred thousand times at night."
And in the *Kulikātantra*:
"Those who delight in the state of a beast (*paśubhāva*) and who are solely of the nature of beasts should never touch the mantra or the rosary at night— at midnight."
Being completely full-bodied, supporting her broad hips, and attached to the pleasures of youth;
being thoroughly and perfectly stout, engaged in sexual union with a young woman who likewise possesses broad hips,
he becomes filled with bliss— naked, sky-clad, with disheveled hair.
With disheveled hair, meditating upon you— who are eternally devoted to the bliss of amorous play together with Mahākāla—
contemplating you within his own heart and visualizing you before his eyes, he recites your mantra, that king of mantras previously mentioned. All the hosts of perfected beings (siddhas)...

All accomplishments (sarvārthasiddhi) come under the control and become subject to that heroic practitioner (vīrasādhaka). And being a poet (kavi), he lives for a very long time, extending over a vast duration, upon the earth. || 10 ||
An explanation of the essential nature. || 10 ||

In this regard, the practitioner of *layayoga* describes: "O Mother, O Janani! If the devotee—the yogi and practitioner intent on divine conduct—remains awake during the night [that which is night for all beings, therein the self-controlled one is awake—Bhagavad Gītā]," then...
The meaning is: being awakened during the "night" characterized by the knowledge of Brahman—the night of all beings;
[he who is] entirely devoted to the pleasures of women endowed with youth, full breasts, and broad hips.
Having attained the *yonimudrā*, one becomes oneself composed of *śakti* for all those situated in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
One should sport with the Supreme Self through the aesthetic sentiment of love (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) alone. Having become full of bliss, one attains oneness with Brahman. — *Gheraṇḍasaṃhitā*
And so it is said in the Gorakṣa-rahasya:

"Having raised the Śakti together with the Jīva to the lotus of the head, having himself become composed of Śakti, one attains union with Paraśiva; this is the play consisting of the bliss of [the state of] Nāda."

One should contemplate the supreme state. While causing the individual soul (jīvātman) to merge into the Supreme Self (paramātman) together with the power of the Kulakuṇḍalinī— who is the eternal youth, the progenitor and protector of living beings— one should meditate here upon her as bearing breasts and hips.

One should meditate upon the goddess Kuṇḍalinī, who is the very form of one’s chosen deity (iṣṭadeva), eternally sixteen years of age, possessing full and firm breasts, dark-complexioned, subtle, the embodiment of creation, and whose nature consists of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe. [Tantrakalpadruma]
By this, the agency of the Kulakuṇḍalinī in the creation and maintenance of the worlds is indicated. "Vivāsāḥ" means one whose covering of māyā has departed;
thus, the sense is that he is awakened (prabuddha).
(18) *Galitacikuraḥ*: one whose *cikuratva*—that is, fickleness—has fallen away or vanished;
being one of steady mind, [he beholds] you together with Paramaśiva.
The meaning is that one who, contemplating you— who are devoted to the bliss of *sāmarasya*— mentally recites your king of mantras,

becomes a knower of reality (*tattvajñānin*) and attains a long life equal to that of the Divine Current (*divyaugha*), the Siddha Current (*siddhaugha*), and the Human Current (*mānavaugha*). All [this is true].

Regarding the "streams of Siddhas" (*siddhaughāḥ*), it should be understood that by the use of the plural number here, the inclusion of the divine (*divya*), perfected (*siddha*), and human (*mānava*) streams is intended. || 10 ||
If one who has become steady and composed recites [the mantra] while constantly contemplating you as the supreme Mahākāla in the act of union,
then for that wise man wandering upon the surface of the earth, [you] shall be submissive in his lotus-hand.
The wives of the Destroyer of Cities are streams of accomplishments. || 11 ||
The commentary (ṭīkā) and the explanation of the essential nature (svarūpavyākhyā). || 11 ||

O Consort of the Destroyer of Cities! O Beautiful One, Destroyer of Tripura! My dear one, having become well-established—calm, pure, moderate in diet, sleeping on the ground, devoted, self-controlled, free from dualities, steady-minded, silent, and with a restrained self—one should perform the recitation (*japa*). (From the *Kulārṇava Tantra*)

With a steady mind, at the beginning of the recitation, one should meditate upon you— who are free from delusion, yet who have assumed a form that appears contrary [to your true nature], who are intensely engaged in the great sexual union with Mahākāla, the Lord of Desire, who are utterly devoted to the bliss of passion, and whose face is turned toward the process of emanation.

One should meditate upon Śivā and, at the conclusion of meditation, recite [the mantra] again. Endowed with both recitation and meditation, the practitioner attains success quickly. [From the Kaulābalī Tantra:
Being thus, while contemplating the meaning of the mantra, for a full year—that is, throughout the entire year—one should always, at all times, [practice].

Having reflected upon you and meditating, one recites [the mantra] mentally. The mental recitation (*mānasa*) consists of contemplating the syllables of the mantra; it is known that a verbal recitation (*vācika*) is equal to one hundred [mental recitations], while a whispered recitation (*upāṃśu*) is one hundred and one times that.
Therefore, the mental recitation is declared to be four times more excellent than the whispered. — *Kaulāvalī*

[The Tantra: He performs the recitation of your mantra. Then, for that wise scholar dwelling upon the surface of the earth, moving about on the ground, the accomplishments (siddhis) are bound within his lotus-hand, in the palm of his lotus-like hand.

The meaning is that the multitude of powers of Śrīvidyā, such as the accomplishment of one's desires (icchāsiddhi) and so forth, become subdued— that is, brought under control. In the reading "mahāsiddhinivahāḥ," it means that the collections of great accomplishments known as sālokya, sārūpya, sāyujya, and nirvāṇa come to depend upon him.
This is the meaning; and this is the explanation of its essential nature.
O Mother, you give birth to saṃsāra, you sustain the entire world beginning with the earth,
and at the time of dissolution, you withdraw it; therefore, you are the creator of the three worlds.
Even the Lord of Śrī and even Maheśa [are subject to this]; what more, then, shall I praise you, O All?
And the commentary (*ṭīkā*) is an exposition of its essential nature (*svarūpa*). || 12 ||

O Mother, O progenitor of the worlds! You give birth to, that is, you produce, the *saṃsāra*, the phenomenal expansion of the universe; therefore, you are the Sustainer (*dhātṛ*), meaning you are the creative power of Brahmā. Furthermore, you protect and support the world.

Therefore, for this reason, you are the Lord of the three worlds, the Lord of Śrī, and even Viṣṇu, the sovereign of the three realms; the meaning is that you are Vaiṣṇavī, the power (śakti) who effects the protection of the universe. At the time of universal dissolution—

At the time of the dissolution of the universe, you withdraw the entire world—consisting of the five great elements beginning with earth—and cause it to become dissolved within your own causal body. Therefore, you are Maheśa and you are Rudra as well; the sense is that you are the power of dissolution (*saṃhāra-śakti*). Hence...

How can I praise you, who are the sole cause of the universe and without a second? What description of your true nature can I offer? The sense is that you alone are beyond the reach of speech. As it is said in the *Tripuṭāstotra*:

You are the earth, the Ordainer, and the creator of the universe; you are the waters and Viṣṇu, the protector of the world. You are fire and Rudra, the agitator of the world; you are the embodiment of sovereignty, as well as the forms of space and wind.
And so it is said in another hymn:

"In order to effect the creation, maintenance, and dissolution [of the world], You assume threefold forms; because the world consists of the three qualities (guṇas), Your manifestations are Brahmā, Acyuta, and the Wielder of the Trident. (12)

Many deluded ones serve the hosts of gods who are superior to you; O Mother, they do not know anything at all of the Supreme. I have freely taken refuge in you, the primordial one worshipped by Hari, Hara, Viriñca, and the other deities.
[She who is] intent upon the great bliss of the delight of passion. || 13 ||
The commentary and the explanation of its essential nature. || 13 ||

O Mother, many—indeed, numerous—are those people who, being utterly deluded and devoid of discernment, worship and propitiate hosts of deities superior to you; yet those people do not attain even the slightest bit of the supreme [goal]. (From the *Kūrma Purāṇa*)
The venerable Kūrma said: That which is determined by the exponents of Brahman in all the Vedas and Vedāntas is the one, all-pervading, subtle, immutable, immovable, and eternal;
it is the infinite, imperishable, absolute, partless, and supreme Brahman—[that] the yogis [realize].
They behold the supreme state of the Great Goddess.
The reality that is higher than the highest, eternal, auspicious, and immutable; merged within the infinite primordial nature—that is the supreme state of the Goddess.
Auspicious, stainless, pure, devoid of qualities, and free from duality—
that supreme state of the Goddess is the object of the realization of the Self.
In that very place, the words of the Śrīdevī are as follows:
"That which is my partless form, consisting of pure consciousness, absolute, supreme,
liberated from all limiting adjuncts, infinite, and the immortal state."
That supreme state is attainable through one single knowledge, without affliction;
perceiving only that knowledge, they enter into me alone.
And so it is stated in the *Yoginītantra*:

"The form of supreme bliss is the great cause of the worlds; that form of the Goddess is devoid of rising and setting. [It is] the supreme reality (*paramatattva*). Indeed, they do not know it... [they do not perceive it].

This great ignorance of Mahābrahmā is considered to be this knowledge, Kālikā, which even the lowest of men attains upon reaching, thereby obtaining the liberation of nirvāṇa— [a state] known by the gods such as Hari, Hara, and Viriñca.
And in that *Argalāstotra*:
"O Supreme Goddess, praised by the four-armed [Viṣṇu] and the four-faced [Brahmā]; ...
O Mother, always praised with devotion by Kṛṣṇa along with Śaṅkha... [and so forth].

Having drunk the *kula-rasa*, the hero should cause [the disciple] to attain the excellent meditation on Brahman— the primordial Goddess who is always to be worshipped, who is the original cause of the universe, and who is intent upon the great bliss of the essence of passion (*rati-rasa*).
O Great Goddess, this meditation on Brahman is the cause of the Nirvana of Brahman.

[The Yoginītantra: You, who are worshipped by Brahmā and the other gods, whose nature is consciousness and bliss, and who are devoted to that great bliss which arises from both— namely, dalliance with Mahākāla (including inverted sexual union) and the flavor of drinking wine.
"Of my own accord," that is, excessively; "I have approached," meaning I have come for refuge. || 13 ||

The earth, the water, the pure fire, the wind, and the sky—you alone are the auspicious Kālī, the beloved of Śiva, the all-encompassing one. What praise can be offered to you, O Mother? By your own compassion, be gracious to me who am helpless;
may you be present at every birth, and may there be no further cycle of existence for me.
The commentary and the explanation of its essential nature. || 14 ||

O Kālī, O dispeller of the fear of time! You are the earth, you are the ground, you are the flood of water, you are the fire, and you are the world in its various forms; you are space, you are the ego-principle preceded by the great principle (mahat), and you are indeed the Self.
O Mother, there is nothing whatsoever superior to you even by a single step; O Karālā, who manifests as Kāmarūpa with bared fangs, my offense must be forgiven.
The Guptārṇava Tantra: Earth, water,
fire, wind, and space— the one, non-dual,
auspicious Goddess who bestows liberation and nirvāṇa, and who ordains the welfare of all living beings.

Giriśaramaṇī Śivānī: She who sleeps on the mountain peak (kūṭa) is Giriśa, the immutable Brahman; his beloved is the *hlādinī* power. You are changeless (*nirvikārā*), both one and many, subtle in form and unchanging, [the source] of millions upon millions of universes.

[She] gives birth; [she is] called "the Goddess. By means of her own Māyā, which is most skillful at bringing about the impossible, she consists of the twenty-four principles (tattvas) beginning with Earth; that is the meaning. She is the "entirety," meaning all things, both moving and unmoving.

"Indeed, all this is Brahman"—such is the Vedic revelation (*śruti*). And [it is said] in the *Caṇḍī*: "O Mother, what praise can there be for You, who are the embodiment of all, the Lord of all, and endowed with all powers?
The sense is that no praise of You is possible, since You are the very form of everything. You...

By Your own compassion—Your unique grace—may You be gracious toward me, who am helpless and without means due to a lack of spiritual practices; be pleased with me. The meaning is: may there be no further birth for me within this worldly existence (*saṃsāra*).
The meaning is: "Make me absorbed in your own state of fearlessness. || 14 ||
O Mahākālī, dwelling in the cremation ground, well-composed, with matted hair and wearing a garment of directions,
one who recites your mantra a thousand times for each flower with his own spilled semen,
while intent on meditation upon you, may act as he pleases.
He becomes the sovereign lord of the earth. || 15 ||
Commentary:
O Mahākālī, O power of Mahākāla! Furthermore, that person who dwells in the cremation ground—remaining well-established there, with hair fallen out—should practice as one naked as the directions.
And one should offer a thousand *sūryapuṣpa* flowers.
Having endowed [the mantra] with one's own vigor, one should recite it for each [deity] and perform the fire-oblation;
having meditated upon and worshipped [them] with great devotion, the practitioner of the lineage should recite the hymn of praise.

From the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*: Established in the realm of the departed (pretabhūmi), well-composed, steady-minded, with hair fallen loose and disheveled, wearing the directions as his garment (*digambara*) or clad in the quarters of space (*dikpaṭa*), intent upon meditation on you, [he beholds] your cloud-bodied form, devoid of clothing, and so forth.

While contemplating your gross form and reciting— that is, uttering— your mantra as well as the Queen of Mantras, [the deity] is smeared with that, meaning with one's own fallen virility, that is, one's own spilled semen.
Of the *arkas*, known as *sūryapuṣpa* or *ākanda*,
there are a thousand flowers— that is, ten hundred flowers— each one individually.
The remainder of the sentence is "he gives with you in mind"; that practitioner, by his own will and without effort, becomes a king firmly established upon the earth. || 15 ||
Explanation of the Non-Essential Nature || 15 ||

Furthermore, regarding the divine side: O Mahākālī, you whose form is the Supreme Brahman! That person who, staying in the cremation ground—at which time all beings dissolve into the form of corpses during the great dissolution—is one whose mind is attached to that cremation ground, which is the Supreme Brahman.

The meaning is: one who is devoted to Brahman; "susthaḥ" means one whose mind is steady; "dikpaṭadharaḥ" means one free from the veil of illusion (māyāvaraṇa); and "nirvikāracittaḥ" means one whose mind is free from modification. "Dhyānanirataḥ" means being intent on meditation upon You, that is, contemplating Your nature as Existence-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda). And it has been said in the Rudrayāmala:

A man who takes refuge in the path of the Kula should recite the mantra while taking shelter of her whose nature is consciousness, who is the abode of knowledge, whose form is the bliss of pure awareness, who shines with the luster of ten million lightning flashes, and who is the essential nature of all beings.
Even while reciting your mantra— that is, uttering your king of mantras mentally—
he should offer the stolen lotus-seat with his own emitted semen,
using the nectar fallen from the thousand-petalled lotus; he should offer water for the feet at the two feet, and the mental arghya offering.
One should offer [the oblation]. One should conceive the mind as the flower and conceive the breaths as the incense.
From the lunar vessel of the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), one should satisfy the supreme Tāriṇī. *Mahānirvāṇatantra*.
And when the sun is situated there, one should offer a beautiful arghya.
The flower of inheritance is knowledge and patience; the flower is the restraint of the senses;
the flower is the merit of knowledge and generosity; and the supreme flower is non-violence.

The *ānandapuṣpa* (bliss-flower) should be offered, as well as the flower for the worship of the practitioner. He who offers the ten flowers shall go to the state of the Savior (*tārakāpada*). [From the *Tārārahasya*:
together with that nectar which flows spontaneously from the thousand-petaled lotus.]

A thousand rays of light, like flowers, reside at the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra); through the sacrifice of the sun, O beloved, the mind dwells in the moon and fire, which is life itself—thus it is stated in the Jñānasaṃkalinī Tantra.
And so it is stated in the Yājñavalkya-saṃhitā:
"The moon is to be known as being in the iḍā [nāḍī], and the sun is heard to be in the piṅgalā.
And it is said in the Prāṇāgnihotra:
And that [fire] named Sūryya is in the form of the solar orb, surrounded by a thousand rays,
and stands upon the head as a single seer through devotion;
these are the forms of the mental modifications arising from the consciousness known as Āditya.

The flowers of his inner being— consisting of compassion, wisdom, patience, and so forth— he offers to you one by one according to the ritual of mental worship, dedicating them to you within the fire of consciousness. That divine practitioner stands firmly upon the earth, acting according to his own will.
Having become the lord of the functions of the senses and so forth belonging to the earthly body of the earth,
the innate state arises of its own accord for the yogi whose power of consciousness has emerged and whose karma has been entirely abandoned.
Kālikā attains attenuation through the illumination of the sun of consciousness. — Mahopaniṣad.

The supreme state is the innate (sahaja), the middling is meditative concentration (dhyāna-dhāraṇā), the inferior consists of recitation and praise, and the lowest consists of fire-offerings and worship. [As stated in the Kulārṇava: "One attains [the goal]"—this is the intended meaning. || 15 ||

On a Tuesday at midday, having recited the mantra even once with love, one should offer upon the funeral pyre the hair from one's head— hair whose vigor has been drained by household chores and which has fallen out— along with its roots.
O Kālī, the excellent poet, firm upon the earth, constantly goes forth mounted upon an elephant.

Commentary: O Kālī, destroyer of Time! That person who is a hero-practitioner (*vīrasādhaka*)—in this house, that is, in this chamber of passion (*madanāgāra*), where the semen has been gathered with a broom—the broom is the *liṅga*.

The semen emitted through pleasure by one's own power, as well as the hair along with its root— that is, the hair uprooted together with the root— on Tuesday, on the day of Mars, at midday, whatever sacrifice, hair, and semen were cast into the broom.
With disheveled hair and the quarters of space for clothing, preceded by the root mantra.

Having performed a *homa* at midnight in a cremation ground on a Tuesday, whoever recites the *Sahasranāma* shall effect the summoning of the lords of the earth. [This is the secret of the *kakāra-kūṭa*. Whether during the middle of the day or at midnight, with love and devotion toward you—

O Goddess of the gods, O Beloved, having recited the *manu* mantra even once over the funeral pyre in the cremation ground, one may sport for a mere moment with Sadāśiva; at that very instant, O Supreme Goddess, nectar (*amṛta*) is produced.

O Goddess, that nectar arising from it, joined with lac-dye—O Mistress of the Gods, one should satisfy the Supreme Deity with that nectar. [Gandharvamālikā: Even if he offers it to you or presents it to you but once, that person is certainly an excellent and true poet.
Being the best among excellent poets, firm as the earth, and a lord of men, he always and at all times goes about— meaning he travels everywhere— mounted upon an elephant. || 16 ||
An explanation of the essential nature. || 16 ||
O Kālī, O dispeller of the fear of death! That practitioner who delights in divine conduct,
within his home— the abode of Brahmā which is the thousand-petaled lotus—
[should contemplate] the semen that has flowed down by means of the broom [of the breath], produced from the union with the Supreme Śiva and Kulakuṇḍalinī.
Vīryāmṛta (p.
The mind, together with its root—the hair on the head—and accompanied by fluctuations such as restlessness, [is described] on Tuesday.
On Tuesday at midday, during the second watch (prahara), whether by night or by day, with supreme love and devotion, having recited your mantra even once— even a single time—
one offers [the oblation] into the funeral pyre, which is your own nature as pure consciousness, and causes it to dissolve into you.
Seedless samādhi: seedless samādhi [is so called] because of the cessation of all mental fluctuations.
[From the Pātañjala-sūtra: It means "he performs"; the sense is that he attains both worldly enjoyment (bhukti) and liberation (mukti). || 16 ||

O wonder! If a devotee, meditating again and again upon the temple of the Flower-Bowed God (Kāmadeva), strewn with its own flowers, recites your mantra before it, he becomes the lord of the hosts of Gandharvas,
a great ocean for the river of the nectar of poetry, and ultimately attains absorption in the supreme state.
Commentary: O Mother, the devoted practitioner (vīrasādhaka), if [the place] is strewn with his own flowers— [as stated in the Mātṛkābhedatantra regarding the first [offering] of a married maiden...]
In the *Ṛtusaṃbhava*: "O Great Goddess, that which has been refined is one's own flower, which deludes all."
He who recites ten thousand [times] while meditating upon the vulva of a woman covered in pollen will certainly delight people with beautiful poetry. [From the *Tantrakalpadruma*:
The abode of the Flower-Bowed God (Kāmadeva), filled with self-arisen flowers, is the yoni before one.

O Agni, meditating upon you again and again, reflecting repeatedly, he recites your mantra ten thousand times; oh, how wonderful! He is the lord of the Gandharva lineage, the most excellent of singers.
The ocean of the rivers of the nectar of poetry— the lord of those rivers of poetic nectar— is the receptacle of all poetry; at the end, upon the dissolution of the body,
he prevails as one merged into your supreme state, having dissolved into your exalted station.
The meaning is that he becomes capable of performing such tasks as creation and so forth. || 17 ||
An explanation of the essential nature. || 17 ||
In this [work], the practice of Yonimudrā is described. And it is said in the Śāktāgama:
"He who does not know the meaning of the mantra, the consciousness of the mantra, and the Yonimudrā—his knowledge does not succeed even by ten million or a hundred million recitations."
O Mother, if a devotee, a practitioner of divine conduct, a yogi, or a spiritual aspirant [worships] with his own flowers, [the Linga] which is established as the form of the self-manifested Liṅga;
The temple of the Flower-Bowed One (Kusumadhanus) is either the triangular mandala situated at the *mūlādhāra* or the triangular mandala situated within the heart-lotus (*hṛtpadma*).
And it is said in the *Śivasamhitā*:
In that foundational lotus, within the pericarp, there exists a most beautiful triangular yoni,
which is concealed in all the tantras.
Furthermore, in that same fourth chapter:
"Having meditated upon Kāma situated in the womb of Brahmā, resembling a bandhūka flower,
radiant as ten million suns, and as cooling as ten million moons."
Above that, however, is the subtle crest (śikhā), the supreme digit whose nature is consciousness;
one should contemplate oneself as being covered by it and become one with it.
And so it is stated in the *Tārārahasya*:
"One should meditate within one's own heart upon the supreme Yoni-maṇḍala,
which is triangular, endowed with all colors, and filled with the [five] elements."
Meditating and contemplating upon [the deity] before one’s own face, and visualizing within that [deity] the form composed of your mantra; as it is said in the *Bhūtaśuddhi-tantra*:
Whichever mantra it may be, and whichever deity is prescribed for it, one should perform the recitation mentally while visualizing that deity's form with the mind.

And in the Kulārṇava: "O Dear One, one who is established in That, whose life-breath is gone to You, whose mind is fixed on That, and whose ultimate refuge is That— performing the contemplation of the meaning of that state, he should mutter the mantra."
He recites your mantra, your king of mantras, very slowly; he recites it mentally.
And it is said in that very place: "It should be recited very slowly, neither too fast nor too slow.
There is nothing higher than song for that lord of the Gandharva ranks, the best of singers."
Because it is seen thus; or else, like Citraratha, the king of the Gandharvas;

furthermore, he becomes like the great poet Kālidāsa, who was a river of the nectar of poetry; moreover, at the end—that is, at the conclusion of the body—he is absorbed into the supreme state (as stated in the Devīgītā).
The Goddess’s words: "At that very moment, his dissolution shall occur within my form, which is pure consciousness alone."
Furthermore, this should be seen in the commentary on verse 13.

The sense is that, having dissolved into You who are of the nature of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*), one attains the state of liberation (*nirvāṇapada*). Regarding the fruit of the practice of *yonimudrā*, it is stated in the *Śivasamhitā*:
"Success arises from practice; through practice one attains liberation. Thus [it is said]. 17.
On the seat of the fifteen-spoked [mandala], upon the heart of a corpse and a *śiva*, she whose face is smiling,
who is intensely devoted to the beauty of the essence of passion with Mahākāla, is embraced at night—
O Mother, even a person who is himself devoted to the bliss of passion, if he should meditate upon you, he would become the destroyer of Smara (Śiva). 18.

Commentary: O Mother, O Janani! That person who is a practitioner (sādhaka), being devoted at night—that is, during the night—with a mind attached to you, and who himself is likewise intent upon the bliss of delight;
Being endowed with the bliss of union (*suratānanda*), the practitioner of mantra should first project a triangle upon the *tripañcarī* seat;
having projected that triangle, he should then project another triangle outside of it. Thereafter, the practitioner of mantra should indeed draw this most excellent pair of triangles.
In the center, however, one should place the Vaindava-cakra, adorned with the seed-syllable and Māyā; outside the six corners, a circle, and beyond that, one should set down an eight-petalled lotus.
"Endowed with an external arrangement and joined by a single city-diagram (bhūpura), one who knows this king of yantras attains liberation; of this there is no doubt. [Kālītantra:
"In the yantra consisting of fifteen triangles, upon the heart of the corpse-Śiva—that is, the heart of Sadāśiva in the form of a corpse—"

The practitioner should meditate upon you— smiling with a radiant countenance, together with Mahākāla, the Supreme Śiva; intensely and utterly devoted to the beauty of the essence of passion, and absorbed in the sweetness of inverted lovemaking— and by so contemplating you, he shall become the Destroyer of Smara himself.
The meaning is that he shall become auspicious. || 18 ||
An explanation of the essential nature. || 18 ||
O Mother, our progenitor! That person who, at night—at midnight—[is as it is said:
"intent on meditation during the Brāhma-muhūrta of the great night"—[attains] that form.
Then one certainly beholds supreme bliss.

Attached to you with one-pointed mind, even by his own self, he who is devoted to the bliss of delight shall, having attained the *yonimudrā*, himself become composed of power (*śakti*). Through the aesthetic sentiment of love (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) alone, he shall sport within the Supreme Self; having become composed of bliss, he shall abide therein.

Oneness may arise in Brahman. [Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā: Having taken recourse to Yonimudrā, having himself become composed of Śakti, and being intent on the bliss of absorption in the form of merger with the Supreme Self—this is the meaning. On the seat of fifteen spokes (tri-pañcāre pīṭhe).
Likewise, the wheel consisting of mantra is the supreme body of the deity;
it is composed of Śiva and Śakti, having the form of a yantra and the nature of Brahman.
But the machine known as one's own body is considered superior to all other machines. [Gandharvatantra:

It is encircled by the functions whose nature is ignorance (avidyā), endowed with eight petals consisting of the eight primordial elements beginning with earth, and possessed of the five organs of knowledge.

[It is] adorned with the seed-syllable consisting of the *bindu*, which is the nature of consciousness reflected therein, characterized by a triangle formed by the five organs of action and the five vital breaths (*prāṇa*), whose essence is pure *sattva*,
and which consists of the five elements beginning with earth— namely, earth, water, fire, air, and...
"Ether, mind, and intellect, as well as ego—this is my second nature, divided eightfold. (Gītā). And likewise in the Gandharva Tantra:
Consisting of the five vital breaths, mind, intellect, and endowed with the ten sense organs, it arises from the unquintuplicated elements; this subtle body is the instrument for experience.
The limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is said to be the causeless form of beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā-nirvāṇākāraṇa*).
Discern the Self as distinct from this triad of adjuncts. [This means] within the machine of one's own body, which is provided with the city of the earth (*bhūpura*).
27) Abiding in the heart of Śiva— who, like a corpse, is inactive— in the state of her own Nirguṇa-Brahman, she [is endowed] with will, action, and knowledge.

The meaning is that, through *māyā* and by means of the division of Śiva and Śakti, she becomes twofold like the form of a fierce crow (*caṇḍakāka*). By Mahākāla, [she who is] intensely devoted to the beauty of the essence of passion—
[that supreme Śakti, who always assumes universal forms by her own will, having cast herself down...]
At that time, a desire for union arose in the Puruṣa.
Then the Goddess herself, having ascended, is established upon Bhairava;
through the abundance of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), they both increase their own bliss.
She is eternally joined with the Supreme Śiva, the Brahman-with-attributes (*saguṇabrahma*), in the state of *viparīta-bhāva* (the inverted posture).

He who meditates upon you, whose face is smiling and who are eternally composed of bliss, as the embodiment of Brahman— or rather, who remembers himself as being identical with her through the state of non-duality; he,
endowed with the realization of non-duality and having made his own body the triple city (tripurī), should worship the Goddess within his very self.

One should meditate upon you as non-different from one's own self, because you abide within the machine of one's own body in the form of the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) through ritual services according to the rules. As it is said in the *Devīmāhātmya*: [The *Gandharvatantra*: Because [the Goddess] exists in the machine of one’s own body in the form of the reflection of consciousness, one should contemplate her as non-different from one’s own self.
And it is stated in the *Devīmāhātmya*:
The Goddess who resides in all beings in the form of a shadow;
and in the Gandharva-tantra:
"One's own Self, which is Tripurāraja, is untainted, devoid of qualities, and pure."
By contemplating [the object] as non-different from oneself, a person attains identity with it.

The meaning is that the practitioner, becoming endowed with the state of non-duality and having merged into You, the Supreme Self, shall become the destroyer of Smara (the god of love) and attain the state of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*). || 18 ||

O Goddess with beautiful hair, may the attainment of every unprecedented perfection at every step be granted to the virtuous dwelling in the mortal world who offer, for Your worship, the bones of a cat, or even its dung, as well as those of a black cat, a camel, a goat, a sheep, a human, or a buffalo.
It prevails. || 19 ||
Commentary:
O Asitā, O Kālikā! In your worship—that is, in the occasional ritual adoration—[one should offer] a cat [endowed with bones, marrow, skin, and blood;
for the word *nāmbha* refers to the cat and the sheep].
Whoever should offer an oblation of a camel and even a buffalo, for him there is no mother;
she is like a mother, acting for his welfare. [In the *Śvāmārahasya*:
regarding the cat, the camel belonging to the cat, the goat belonging to the camel, and the human and buffalo belonging to the goat.

Or else, let them freely and at their own will offer as a sacrificial oblation (bali) the flesh (palala), that is, meat, which is excellent and accompanied by hair and bone, belonging either to a human bull (naramahiṣa) or to a goat (chāga).
For practitioners, at every step and at every stage, all kinds of unprecedented and marvelous accomplishments— the fruitfulness of their actions— arise and are brought to perfection (p.
An explanation of the essential nature. || 19 ||

O Asitā—[the root √siṅ means "to bind"; the past passive participle is *sita*. According to Amara, *asita* means "bound" or "white. Here, *asitā* means one whose nature is eternally liberated (*nityamukta-svabhāvā*). In your worship—that is, in the ritual of the internal sacrifice, meaning mental worship—[may there be success].

One should worship the six enemy-animals, such as cats and others—possessing fur, bones, and flesh, and complete with all their limbs—by offering a goat as a sacrificial oblation (*bali*). [In the *Annadākalpa*: "Having offered the goat, which is Desire (*kāma*), as a sacrifice, one should worship. The meaning here is that the goat represents Desire.

Buffalo is anger, cat is greed, man is pride, ram is delusion, camel is envy; these are to be understood through the similarity of their qualities. For those offering the oblation: "With the mind as the ladle, one should offer the sacrifice of dharma and adharma into the fire of the self, which is kindled by the oblation."
I constantly offer the functions of the senses into the path of the Suṣumṇā; Svāhā!

O Vṛhannīla! For those virtuous people of good character dwelling among mortals who, desiring the destruction of lust and other passions, offer [their senses] to You, whose nature is consciousness, in the form of an oblation of worship— at every step, at every stage, in due order— [may there be success].
This is the meaning: "unprecedented" means the most excellent; "all success" refers to the fivefold liberation [as stated in the Śrīśivagītā:
"Know that liberation, O Rāghava, is fivefold: sālokya, sārūpya, sāmīpya, sāyujya, and kaivalya"].
"Prabhavati" means they attain preeminently; the meaning is that practitioners of this kind obtain such liberations as *sālokya* and the others. || 19 ||

One who is self-controlled, devoted to eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), and skilled in meditating upon the pair of your feet during the day, should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; then at night, naked and engaged in the pleasure of sexual union,
he should likewise recite it one hundred thousand times, and he shall become equal to Śiva, the Destroyer of Smara.
Upon the surface of the earth. || 20 ||
Commentary: O Mother, that person who is self-controlled (vaśī), having conquered the senses, and devoted to eating sacrificial food (haviṣyāśanarata)—
who, while devoted to eating sacrificial food, should recite the mantra while remembering the Goddess by day and at night—
Attached to amorous dalliance, that lord of the earth shall become the possessor of a hundred thousand [gold pieces]. [From the *Tantra-kalpadruma*:

At the conclusion of the recitation, being one who eats sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), and during the day—day after day—skilled in meditation upon the pair of your lotus feet, [he should remain] intent on the contemplation of your two lotus feet.
Being devoted to solitude, he recites the mantra one hundred thousand times;
furthermore,
at night, he remains naked and unclothed.
Through the diversion of sexual union; *nidhuvana* means "trembling" and is neuter in the sense of "sexual pleasure."

Being distinguished by the joy of sexual union, he should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times (*lakṣa*); on the surface of the earth, he shall become equal to the Destroyer of Smara (Śiva). In the reading *samyak*, however—
The meaning is: having recited [the mantra] beginning with *setu*, *mahāsetu*, *kulluka*, and *āṭika* according to the prescribed procedure.
This is the explanation of the essential nature [of the mantra]. 20. 20.

The practitioner who has conquered his senses, who subsists on sacrificial food (haviṣya), and who is devoted to single-minded contemplation of your lotus feet during the day, should recite your mantra one hundred thousand times; furthermore, at night, he should do so according to the Kula practice while naked.

The meaning is that he is free from the veil of *māyā* and is changeless. Furthermore, by means of the "delight of union" (*nidhuvanavinoda*)—as stated in the *Kulārṇava*: "That which consists of the blissful fullness arising from the union of the supreme Śakti and the Self as a couple is true sexual union (*maithuna*); others are merely those who indulge with women."—he remains thus.
The meaning is that, being distinguished by that [practice] and delighting in the bliss of union with the consort who is one's own supreme power (*paraśakti*),
he should mutter your mantra one hundred thousand times; such a person shall be equal to Smarahara (Śiva) upon this earth.
The meaning is that he becomes one who is liberated while living (jīvanmukta), equal to Śiva. || 20 ||
O Mother, this hymn of yours, known as *Manusamuddhāraṇajanusvarūpā*,

which includes the ritual for worshipping your pair of lotus feet— whosoever recites it at midnight or during the time of worship, even if they are merely prattling, the nectar-like essence of poetic genius flows forth from them. (21)

Commentary: O Mother, as for that person— whoever it may be— your "birth" (*januḥ*) refers to your birth for the purpose of the "extraction" (*samuddhāraṇa*), that is, the perfect extraction, of your *manus*, which are the mantras.

That from which [this work] originates; that which is joined with the ritual procedure for worshipping the pair of your lotus feet—that is, accompanied by the rules for the worship of your glorious lotus feet; called "Svarūpa"—that is, the form (rūpa) of your own nature (svarūpa), of your very self (ātman), which is inherently devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).

"The knowers of Brahman understand that very realization of the oneness of the individual soul and Brahman—the awareness 'I am He'—to be the meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa). — *Śivārcanacandrikā*.
This is the designation of meditation consisting of the gross, subtle, causal, and fourth (turya) states, according to their distinction as having attributes (saguṇa).
That in which there is this narration;
30) this hymn [is to be recited] at midnight, the middle of the night, or during the time of worship.
With reference to this, he recites: "O Goddess, a hymn recited mentally or even muttered with speech—both are fruitless, like water in a broken vessel."
Viśuddheśvara! He utters aloud:

his prattle, though consisting of meaningless words, is the nectar-essence of poetry, by the single recitation of which all obstacles become agitated and perish on every side, like moths in a blazing fire.

His speech, consisting of prose-lotuses, flows like the current of the Gaṅgā; [in the *Kālīkulasarvasva*] it means that his speech, full of the nectar-taste of poetry, spreads forth and issues out. || 21 ||
A multitude of fawn-eyed women, trembling with love, follows him;

even the lord of the earth, a veritable counterpart of Kubera, remains under his sway. His enemy experiences imprisonment through his playful pastimes, and that devotee prevails as one liberated while living throughout every birth.
And the commentary is an exposition of the essential nature [of the work]. || 22 ||
A multitude of deer-eyed women— a group of beautiful fawn-eyed ladies—
follows that practitioner, moving restlessly with affection;
even the lord of the earth, the master of the land, is under his sway, having become subject to him, as is the representative of Kubera.
He becomes wealthy, equal to Kuvera; yet his enemy considers that reciter of this hymn to be as terrifying as a prison. Such a person is devoted to you in birth after birth.

Being full of devotion, by means of playful pastimes (*kelikalayā*), he effortlessly becomes liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) and liberated after death (*videhamukta*). Alternatively, that devotee, through playful pastimes— that is,
through the delight of sport— remains alive for a long time, throughout an extended duration.

Holding [this in mind], at the end of the body, having attained liberation, he becomes one whose birth has ceased for every future life—that is, one free from rebirth—and attains the nirvāṇa of Brahman. [This is the hymn proclaimed by Mahākālarudra; one should always recite it with a spirit of devotion.]
The devotee who studies this shall not suffer from grief, nor shall he be subject to disease or death;
in the end, he attains perfection and the realization of absolute liberation (kaivalya). [Mahākālasaṃhitā]—the sense is that he reaches [the goal]. 22.
Thus ends the hymn entitled *Svarūpa*, composed by the venerable Mahākāla in praise of the venerable Dakṣiṇākālī.

The commentary bestowing stainless bliss and the explanation of the essential nature are hereby completed. She who is Kālī, the beloved of Time, who dispels impurity when invoked as the Destroyer of Time;
she who is Tārā by form, honored by the Lotus-born Brahmā, the supreme knowledge of Brahman; she who is Śrīvidyā...

May that Goddess, who is the path to liberation for practitioners, who is measured by Hari and Hara, who exists in all forms for the benefit of seekers, and who is the Mother, grant auspiciousness to those who offer her praise.
By that very king of hymns which was described by Mahākāla, the true nature of Kālikā is revealed, which bestows bliss upon her devotees.
This hymn, beginning with *karpūra* and permeated by spiritual impressions (*vāsanā*), has been explained by me through another interpretation,
adorned with simple meanings;
it was composed by me in the Śaka year [measured as] one hundred and seventy-eight (178) for the benefit of practitioners.
For the sake of awakening, by the Lord Vimalānanda.
This commentary, which possesses a corresponding meaning and bestows stainless bliss, shall always shine upon the throats of even those devotees who merely read it.

In the city of Koṭālipāḍa, in the lineage of Śunaka, was Harihara, a lord of the assembly and the greatest among the great; his son was the noble Kāliprasāda, born of that same family; and his son was Raghuvarṇin, who performed all prescribed rites.
His son was Vimalānandasvāmī, who followed in his footsteps; he was known as Satīśacandra Rāya and was adorned with the title of Caudhurī.
May this commentary on the *Karpūrādistotra*, composed by that same author for the delight of the learned, endure and serve also to please the goddess Kālikā.
Oṃ tat sat oṃ.
